title: Your Phone's GPS Would Be Off by Miles a Day Without Einstein
fb_caption: The blue dot on your map depends on clocks more than twelve thousand miles up. Your phone times signals from at least four GPS satellites to work out where you are, but up there weaker gravity makes clocks tick faster, and even after their speed slows them a bit they gain about 38 millionths of a second a day. Signals move at light speed, so left uncorrected that tiny gap would add up to miles of error in a single day. That's why the satellite clocks are tuned to tick slightly slow before launch. Blue dot or street signs: which do you trust?
engagement_comment: Blue dot or street signs: which do you trust? 1 = the blue dot, always, 2 = street signs, 3 = both, just in case.

tts.director_notes: Calm, curious American male explainer, warm and clear, about 170 words per minute, short pause before the twist. Read only the script text.

beats.text: Your phone's blue dot stays on your street thanks to Albert Einstein.
It listens to GPS satellites over twelve thousand miles up, each with an atomic clock.
It times signals from at least four of them to work out where you are.
Here's the twist. Up there, weaker gravity makes clocks run fast. Speed slows them slightly, but they gain about thirty-eight millionths of a second a day.
Signals move at light speed, so that adds up. Uncorrected, your dot could drift miles in a day.
So the clocks are tuned to tick slightly slow before launch, and your dot stays put.
Blue dot or street signs: which do you trust? Tell us below.
